e.t: Beth Hoglah is a Hebrew place-name, rendered as “Beth” and “Hoglah.” It identifies a location rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract idea. The name occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Joshua, where it appears in descriptions of territorial boundaries and locations. Its precise significance in each passage comes from the surrounding boundary description, but its normal function is to name the place Beth Hoglah.

Bilgai is a personal name, rendered “Bilgai.” It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, object, or doctrine. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this name occurs once, at Nehemiah 10:8. The available wording identifies the person by name, but without the surrounding verse text it does not establish the individual’s role or provide a broader meaning for the name. Thus, Bilgai is best understood simply as the proper name of a person mentioned in that passage.

Its exact significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies a valley.

This Hebrew word means “shut.” It functions as a verb describing closing something, so that access or passage is no longer open. In the Old Testament, it occurs once, at Nehemiah 7:3. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in Isaiah 27:9. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage, but its ordinary lexical sense is straightforward: stones. The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Leviticus 19:24 and Judges 9:27, so its basic meaning is clear even though its precise force depends on each passage. In its recorded uses, it functions as something that can be offered, brought, or shared in relation to God and communal rejoicing.

In that occurrence, it functions as the object of the sentence—the thing connected with the action being described—rather than naming a person or an action. Its basic sense is therefore a ruined condition, while the surrounding verse determines the specific reference and force of the word there.

In the Hebrew Bible corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Ezra 10:43. Its precise significance beyond identifying this person cannot be established from the lexical evidence alone.

e.t: “Ahaziah” is a Hebrew personal name, not a general descriptive word. It identifies people in the Old Testament and is used chiefly in passages about kings and royal family members. The name occurs 37 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across 30 verses, and is rendered “Ahaziah” in the available English renderings. Its role is therefore to name a person; the surrounding passage is needed to determine which individual is meant in a particular occurrence.

This Hebrew word means “thrust,” describing something driven or pushed forcefully. It occurs once in the Old Testament, in Isaiah 14:19. Its wording presents forceful movement rather than gentle placing or ordinary carrying. Because the word appears only once and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise emphasis in that passage depends on the full context. Still, “thrust” gives the clearest supported sense of the word.

Jehud is a Hebrew proper name rendered as “Jehud,” referring to a named place rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract idea. It appears once in the Hebrew Bible data, at Joshua 19:45. Since the word is preserved as a name in English, its meaning is primarily its identification of Jehud itself. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain its specific role in that passage, but the lexical evidence supports understanding it as the name Jehud.

This Hebrew word refers to “mire,” identifying a muddy substance or place in the sentence. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both in Psalms: Psalm 40:2 and Psalm 69:2. In these occurrences, the word names the thing associated with the speaker’s situation, rather than describing an action or a person. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Juttah is a Hebrew place-name, rendered “Juttah.” It functions as a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, both times in Joshua: once at Joshua 15:55 and once at Joshua 21:16. These references establish its repeated biblical usage as the name Juttah, while the surrounding verse context would be needed to explain what is being said about the place in each passage.

This Hebrew term is a place name, rendered “Janoah.” It does not function as an ordinary descriptive word or action in the passages where it appears. The name occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament: twice in Joshua and once in 2 Kings. Its precise significance in each passage comes from the surrounding geographical and historical context, but the lexical evidence identifies it as the name Janoah rather than a general concept or quality.

Its exact significance in any verse comes from the surrounding passage.

Its precise sense in each passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea is a pointed object that can mark, pierce, or secure something.
